title: Quantile and threshold calibration separate even for Gaussian forecasts
shortTitle: Quantile and threshold calibration checks can disagree
oneLine: Passing every quantile calibration check does not mean passing every threshold check, even for smooth Gaussian forecasts: the two checks weight the same probability-zero set of forecasts differently, and errors reach about one percentage point.
abstract: A probabilistic forecast is calibrated when its stated probabilities match what happens. Two widely used checks condition on different summaries of the forecast: on a predicted quantile, or on the predicted probability of staying below a fixed threshold. Gneiting and Resin (2023) proved the two checks equivalent for continuous, strictly increasing forecast distributions that take only countably many values, and conjectured that countability could be dropped; Resin, Yang and Gneiting (2026) still list these implications as conjectures. This candidate shows that countability cannot be dropped. Gaussian forecasts with uniformly distributed location and scale, paired with explicit smooth outcome laws whose densities stay within a factor of two of the forecast densities, separate the checks in both directions: one law passes every conditional quantile check and has an exactly uniform PIT, yet fails threshold and marginal calibration at every threshold; the other passes every threshold check but fails quantile calibration, with a PIT distribution function strictly below the uniform one at every interior level. The errors reach about one percentage point. For outcomes with finitely many ordered values and positive forecast probabilities, conditional exceedance calibration implies threshold calibration when the forecast has countable support or there are at most three values, but not with four or more. For nominal outcomes, full probabilistic calibration implies marginal calibration with a sharp bound, and class-wise calibration does not imply average probabilistic calibration; two further nominal implications are settled for at most three classes or countable support and remain open beyond. The mechanism is the Borel–Kolmogorov phenomenon. Limits: population constructions, not a study of deployed forecasts; the amplitude rests on a computer-assisted interval bound; no finite-sample test theory. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Theorem 3.1 (proof): Gaussian forecasts N(M, S²) with M uniform on [−1, 1] and S uniform on [1, 2], with explicit smooth outcome laws (densities between half and one and a half times the forecast density, perturbation size ε ≤ 1/10): under one law the forecast passes every conditional quantile check with an exactly uniform PIT but fails threshold and marginal calibration at every threshold, P(Y ≤ x) − E F(x) = ε c₀ e^{−x²} with c₀ = 1 − (4/3) log 2; under the other it is threshold calibrated but fails quantile calibration, with PIT CDF strictly below the identity.

Section 3.5 (computation): at ε = 1/10 outcomes fall below 0 with probability 0.50758 while forecasts average 1/2; on a common segment the threshold error is ε/9 ≈ 0.011; a two-sided binomial test at the 5% level with 80% power needs about 34,000 cases to detect the marginal error.

Theorems 4.1–4.3 (proof): for k ordered outcome values with positive forecast probabilities, conditional exceedance calibration implies threshold calibration if the forecast has countable support or k ≤ 3; an explicit four-value forecast with one continuous parameter satisfies conditional exceedance, probabilistic and marginal calibration but not threshold calibration.

Theorems 5.3 and 5.5, Proposition 5.6 (proof): for nominal outcomes, full probabilistic calibration implies marginal calibration, with the sharp bound TV ≤ 2d − d²; class-wise calibration does not imply average probabilistic calibration, with all probabilities positive; fCC ⇒ fTC and pCC ⇒ pTC hold for k ≤ 3 or countable support and remain open for four or more classes.

Theorems 6.1 and 7.1 (proof): in location–scale families every compactly supported perturbation preserving either property is described by one differential operator; in any smooth family the two conditional laws on a common fibre differ by the forecast-density factor, so they agree for every outcome law only if that density is constant on the fibre.

narration: Two calibration checks that are not the same: an Evidence Press briefing. Many forecasts are probability distributions, like a weather service's spread of possible temperatures or a machine-learning model's prediction. A forecast is calibrated if its probabilities can be taken at face value. Forecasters check this in two standard ways. A threshold check fixes a value, say thirty degrees, and asks whether the stated chances of staying below it come true. A quantile check fixes a probability, say one half, and asks whether outcomes fall below the forecast median half of the time. For a smooth forecast, the two questions pick out exactly the same forecasts, so passing one kind of check should mean passing the other. Gneiting and Resin proved this when forecasts take only countably many shapes, and conjectured that the restriction could be dropped; a later overview by Resin, Yang and Gneiting still lists it as open. This candidate shows that it cannot. With ordinary bell-curve forecasts whose centre and spread vary smoothly, it builds outcomes that pass every quantile check exactly, with a perfectly flat histogram of probability integral transforms, yet fail every threshold check; and other outcomes that do the reverse. The errors reach about one percentage point. In one example, outcomes fall below zero fifty point seven six percent of the time, while the forecasts say fifty percent on average. Spotting that needs about thirty-four thousand forecast cases, an ordinary verification sample. Why does this happen? Both checks look at the same set of forecasts, but that set has probability zero, and the two checks weight its members differently. One weights them evenly, the other by their spread. The same error then averages to nothing under one weighting and to one ninth of the perturbation under the other. This is the classical Borel–Kolmogorov paradox. The paper also settles the case of outcomes with a few ordered categories: the quantile-type check implies the threshold check when there are at most three categories, but can fail once there are four or more of them. For unordered categories, it proves one further conjecture from that overview, gives a cleaner counterexample to another, and partly settles two more, which stay open for larger numbers of categories. The practical message: run both kinds of check. These are constructed examples, not a study of real forecasting systems. Evidence Press published this anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, and its review was internal, not peer review. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

internalReplay.note: All three scripts were rerun from fresh copies in normal mode and under python -O with pinned packages; every recorded output matched byte for byte. Lowering the certified bound to 4.7 and swapping two table entries of the four-value construction each make the checks fail under -O. GitHub CI reruns the exact discrete checks, the certificate and both negative controls (blocking) and the Gaussian checks (non-blocking) on Linux.
